title: One More Descent
subtitle: Field Notes No. 003: four roguelike traditions, four prices for dying
rightsNotice: Game images and quoted material belong to their respective rights holders. Included for commentary and criticism; no endorsement or ownership is implied.
editorial: Field Notes No. 003 is about the moment after a run ends. Every game here is a turn-based dungeon descent, but each answers the genre's central question differently: what survives when you fall? In Azure Dreams the hero forgets every level he gained while the monsters he raised remember theirs, so a failed climb still feeds the stable at home. In Baroque, death takes your items and levels and gives you the next piece of a deliberately withheld story. Sometimes the right move is to die on purpose. Z.H.P. banks every level you earned into a permanent total and hands you a body-shaped grid of chips to wire, which makes it the issue's closest thing to a mech garage and its deepest long-haul game. Pokémon Mystery Dungeon: Explorers of Sky barely punishes failure at all. It's included as the gentle tradition, with an honest warning about its long, earnest dialogue. Each article explains which edition it describes and keeps reviews from release separate from later reassessments and fan reputation; where a contemporary English review doesn't exist, the article says so. Field Notes did not play-test these games on any emulator or device for this issue. Keep paper handy for notes. Two of these games reward remembering who said what after you died.

articles.title: Azure Dreams: The Hero Forgets, the Monsters Remember
articles.deck: Konami's 1998 tower crawler resets Koh to level 1 on every exit and lets his hatched familiars keep everything. Here's how its egg, fusion and Sand economy works, what a death costs, and what to ignore in town.

articles.deck: Sting's surreal roguelike pushes its story forward through your deaths. It reached English as the 2008 Atlus PS2 remake and, much later, as a fan translation of the 1999 PlayStation port. This covers which to play, how VT and item banking work, and why critics split.

articles.deck: Nippon Ichi's 2010 PSP roguelike resets you to level 1 in every dungeon, then turns every failed run into permanent Total Level, bolted-on body parts and chip wiring. It's the issue's deepest build, provided you can stand the comedy.

articles.deck: Chunsoft's Mystery Dungeon engine at its most child-friendly and heavily narrated. Failure costs half your money and a few items, the dialogue never stops, and the Special Episodes are the real draw. Read this before you commit a long session to it.
